fixes.explanation: Close, friend! Asher stands right beside Gad in the list of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:26). But the LORD names Gad. He asks, “Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?” Gad is the one in the question.

A fortress is built up, and this verse is about what gets torn down. The LORD says Rabbah “…will become a heap of ruins…” Its villages will be burned too. A strong city is a natural thing to picture, friend, but that's not what the verse says.

His priests and officials. The LORD says, “…Milcom will go into exile together with his priests and officials.” So the god and the ones named with him go into exile together. The verse names priests and officials, and no one else.

Horses and chariots are a fair guess for a king's company, friend, but the verse doesn't mention them. It says Milcom will go into exile “…together with his priests and officials.” Those are the ones who go along.
Musicians and singers aren't listed, friend. The text says Milcom will go into exile “…together with his priests and officials.” Those are the ones named.

The LORD does say Rabbah will become a heap of ruins (Jeremiah 49:2), but nothing in the passage says it stays empty for good. The LORD says, “Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity…” One word, “Yet,” turns the whole message. The last thing He says about the Ammonites is restoration.

True. The LORD asks, “If those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, can you possibly remain unpunished?” Then He says, “You will not go unpunished, for you must drink it too.” The verse says Edom drinks the cup too.
The heavens aren't named in this oath. The LORD says, “For by Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD…” He swears by Himself. No one else is named.

Fear sounds close to the terror Edom causes, but it isn't the word in the blank. The LORD says, “The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you…” The word that fits is pride. The verse names both the terror and the pride.

True. The LORD says, “Edom will become an object of horror. All who pass by will be appalled and will scoff at all her wounds.” I think this part is heavy, friend. Those passing by are appalled, and they scoff.

The text says the opposite. It speaks of the plans the LORD has drawn up against Edom, and then says, “Surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away…” Their pasture will be made desolate too. I think this is a sad line, and it's not safe for the little ones.

False. The verse speaks of the plans the LORD has drawn up against Edom, and then says, “Surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away; certainly their pasture will be made desolate because of them.” They aren't kept safe. It's a heavy line, friend, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Quake. The passage says, “At the sound of their fall the earth will quake; their cry will resound to the Red Sea.” The earth shakes at the sound of the fall. The cry carries all the way to the Red Sea.
Rejoicing isn't in this verse, friend. The passage says, “At the sound of their fall the earth will quake…” The earth shakes. The cry carries all the way to the Red Sea.
Rest is the opposite of what the verse says. The passage says, “At the sound of their fall the earth will quake…” The sound of Edom's fall shakes the earth. Nothing about it is restful.

That's the picture. The passage says, “In that day the hearts of Edom’s mighty men will be like the heart of a woman in labor.” These are the mighty men, and their hearts are anything but mighty. Notice the word “like.” It's a comparison, and the text doesn't say more than that.

A lion does appear earlier, in verse 19, as a picture of one who comes up against Edom. It's not a picture of Edom's own men. The passage says their hearts will be “…like the heart of a woman in labor.” These mighty men aren't roaring.

Pride does show up in this passage, in verse 16. But the passage doesn't say Edom's mighty men have a king's heart. It says, “In that day the hearts of Edom’s mighty men will be like the heart of a woman in labor.”
